transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Narayanan (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (CTO, Aurora), Jon Park (Lead ML Eng), Eleni Flores (Infra), Samira Khan (Product)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on model selection and deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Key constraints: need for 32k+ context for long docs, multilingual outputs (EN/ES/FR/DE/JP), and tool-calling for internal retrieval and external APIs. Security and audit trail questions for private deployment. Agreed next steps: pricing + perf matrix, 10k token benchmark, share prompts and compliance contacts.

Topics:
- Open model comparisons (Llama-2, MPT, RedPajama, Vicuna variants)
- Context length requirements and chunking strategies
- Multilingual quality and evaluation metrics
- Tool-calling / function calling / external API integrations
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private trade-offs (latency, cost, data residency, KMS)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex with Redwood, this is Priya on the SE side. Um, quick roll call?
[00:12] Marta Ruiz: Hi this is Marta, CTO at Aurora Optics. We got Jon, Eleni and Samira here too. Thanks for making time.
[00:18] Alex Chen: Great. Want to frame the call as model selection + deployment mode — you told us in the form you need long context and multilingual, plus tool calling, is that right?
[00:28] Marta Ruiz: Yeah exactly. Our use case is analytics on multi-page optical design documents and customer support transcripts. So sometimes we need the model to access 20-30k tokens in one shot, and also answer in Spanish or French depending on region.
[00:42] Jon Park: And we want to call internal retrieval APIs — so the model needs tool-calling to fetch product metadata or logs. Latency is a factor but cost is probably the bigger constraint at scale.
[00:52] Priya Narayanan: Cool. So two dimensions: model architecture and deployment. For architecture are you leaning toward big-context open models like 32k LLMs, or are you ok with chunking + retrieval?
[01:05] Jon Park: Prefer native long context if possible — reduces complexity. But we can fall back to retrieval for some tasks. We care about hallucination rates too.
[01:14] Alex Chen: Understood. For open models there are a few profiles to consider: Llama-2-Chat 70B (with 32k variants becoming common), RedPajama variants, MPT-30B-extended, and community fine-tuned Vicuna / Orca forks. Each has tradeoffs — model quality vs cost and availability on our hosted offering.
[01:33] Marta Ruiz: Can you say more about Redwood Hosted availability? If we pick a big 70B 32k model, will it be available on hosted or only on Dedicated/Private?
[01:42] Priya Narayanan: Good question. On hosted we surface curated model variants — some 32k-capable families are available (we've added optimized kernels for a subset). For the largest 70B variants and some bleeding-edge community forks, dedicated capacity is recommended for predictable throughput. Private is possible if you need on-prem or VPC with KMS.
[02:00] Jon Park: Okay. What's the latency delta roughly between hosted optimized 32k model and a dedicated pool?
[02:07] Priya Narayanan: Depends on batch size. For single-user low-batch requests, hosted with dedicated instance-backed pools will be similar to dedicated. If you need sustained concurrency, Dedicated gives you reserved GPU and lower percent tail latency. For an example a 32k-profile 70B on hosted might be 900-1200ms per response token in our benchmarks at small batch, whereas Dedicated with tuned kernels can drop p50 by 15-25%. Those are broad numbers but we can share a perf sheet.
[02:33] Eleni Flores: From infra perspective we need logs, audit trail, and KMS integration. Is the private deployment full air gap or can we run a VPC deployment with Redwood control plane?
[02:43] Alex Chen: Yes both. Private offers a control plane that can be customer-managed over VPC and also an on-prem package for stricter requirements. KMS/HSM integrations are supported and we provide audit logs. We'll share SOC 2 and compliance docs.
[02:55] Samira Khan: For multilingual, do you have evaluation metrics or examples? We need to know performance in Spanish and Japanese for both generation and instruction-following.
[03:04] Priya Narayanan: We do model-wise evals; open models vary. Some RedPajama-forked models have stronger English outperform on instruction tasks after fine-tune, but Japanese can be weaker unless models are trained on multilingual corpora. Llama-2-based models often have decent multilingual capability, and there are specialized multilingual forks. We'll include per-model multilingual BLEU/ROUGE-like scores in the matrix.
[03:26] Jon Park: And tool-calling: do you support both synchronous function-calling and async callbacks? We need to call our retrieval service and also a ticketing API that sometimes times out.
[03:35] Priya Narayanan: Redwood supports function/tool-calling patterns — streaming token events, function call spec, and you can route calls through server-side middleware. For long-running tasks, we recommend an async pattern where the model emits a reference and the infra performs the call and returns result; we can help design the flow.
[03:49] Marta Ruiz: Any limitations for tool calling on hosted vs private?
[03:53] Alex Chen: On hosted you'll use our function-calling interface with configurable outbound network rules. Dedicated/Private gives you more control over VPC egress and you can run the runtime inside your private network for enforced non-egress.
[04:05] Jon Park: Cost - do you bill per token only or are there instance-hour components for dedicated?
[04:10] Alex Chen: Hosted is usage-based (per-token for generations/embeds). Dedicated is reserved capacity: monthly commit + overage. Private is typically licensed with a platform fee + support. We'll share a concrete pricing example tuned to your expected volume.
[04:22] Samira Khan: For chunking fallback: if we can't do native 32k for all flows, what's Redwood's recommendation?
[04:28] Priya Narayanan: Typically hybrid approach: for long analytical reads, run a retrieval-augmented chunking pipeline with overlap + question condensation. For doc-level summarization you can use an initial embedding + top-k retrieval then a synthesis step. But if you want end-to-end single-shot reasoning over 20-32k tokens, choose a long-context model on Dedicated/Private.
[04:50] Marta Ruiz: Is there a difference in hallucination for chunking vs single-shot?
[04:54] Priya Narayanan: Chunking can reduce hallucination if retrieval precision is high; however, context fragmentation can cause coherence issues. We recommend addition of prompt engineering patterns like reference anchors and chain-of-thought suppression for synthesis.
[05:09] Jon Park: About latency again - for the ticketing flow we need sub-second p95 for short responses - is that realistic?
[05:16] Priya Narayanan: For small context and small models, sub-second p95 is achievable in Dedicated. For 32k big models, p95 commonly is higher - depends on token throughput. We can optimize with quantized kernels and batching but there's a tradeoff.
[05:33] Alex Chen: Want to surface a few model recommendations given your constraints: 1) If you want best multilingual + tool-calling with cost sensitivity -> MPT-30B-extended or a quantized RedPajama-3B for most lower-latency tasks and use retrieval for long-docs; 2) If you need single-shot 20-32k context with highest quality -> Llama-2 Chat 70B-32k-like family on Dedicated; 3) If data residency or compliance is hard requirement -> Private deployment with a 70B or 30B tuned profile.
[06:04] Marta Ruiz: We were also evaluating Anthropic and OpenAI; how do you compare on hallucination and compliance?
[06:11] Alex Chen: Many managed providers have strong general models; we differentiate on deployment flexibility and observability - you can run the same API across Hosted, Dedicated, Private. For compliance, we offer private VPC and on-prem options and expanded audit logs. Hallucination varies per model; we provide eval harnesses so you can run your prompts against multiple models side-by-side.
[06:32] Samira Khan: Can we run a side-by-side benchmark? We want to see Spanish/Japanese generation quality and 10k token summarization.
[06:39] Priya Narayanan: Yes - next step we'll run a 10k token benchmark on Hosted and Dedicated nodes and return token latency, cost, and sample outputs. Please share the prompt set.
[06:50] Jon Park: Ok we'll export a representative set and upload to the secure folder. Also want to confirm log retention for Private deployment - we need 2 years for audit.
[06:58] Alex Chen: Our Private options can support that retention and custom S3 retention policies; we'll share the compliance worksheet.
[07:06] Marta Ruiz: A couple of smaller questions - do you support function calling with schema validation?
[07:10] Priya Narayanan: Yes we support typed function spec and enforcement; you can validate outputs server-side and reject malformed call responses.
[07:18] Eleni Flores: Network constraints - if we run Dedicated, can we restrict egress to only certain endpoints?
[07:23] Alex Chen: Yes, we can set egress firewall rules on Dedicated and even stricter on Private. For Hosted ephemeral egress is controlled but Dedicated/Private gives more control.
[07:33] Samira Khan: Any gotchas about fine-tuning or continual learning?
[07:36] Priya Narayanan: We support fine-tuning or instruction-tuning for dedicated customers; you'll want to consider model drift monitoring and the cost of retrain. Redwood Optimize has recommendations on quantization/fine-tune tradeoffs.
[07:48] Marta Ruiz: Sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[07:52] Alex Chen: Recap: Alex will send hosted vs dedicated cost spreadsheet and model perf matrix; Priya will schedule a technical deep dive and run a 10k-token benchmark; Aurora will share prompt set and compliance contacts; we'll also share SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[08:06] Jon Park: Thanks, that works.
[08:09] Marta Ruiz: Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[08:12] Alex Chen: Appreciate your time, we'll follow up this week.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms (e.g., KV cache heard as 'K V cash'), some speaker overlap at the start.
